title: S-M-Ch

segments.voice: Yesterday, K-T-N: katan, small, the lesser light and the boy out with the sheep. Your line was small. You met festival joy and its guest list back on day five hundred; today, the root under it.

"Mazel tov, may we share in many more smachot." It's a line heard at bar mitzvahs, weddings, a baby naming, a family party with too much food. Smachot is the plural of simcha. In everyday Jewish English, a simcha isn't only a feeling. It's an event, with chairs and a caterer and an aunt who cries at the right moment. You don't usually have a simcha alone. And the Torah's instructions about joy come with a guest list.
screen: `MAY WE SHARE IN MANY SMACHOT.` → `A SIMCHA IS AN EVENT.` → `JOY WITH A GUEST LIST.`

segments.voice: S-M-Ch. Sin, mem, chet. Simcha: joy, gladness. Sameach: glad. And the verb, to rejoice. First, joy as a command. Deuteronomy, describing the harvest festival, says: "And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast." It's in the same voice as the other instructions. Some readers ask: how do you command a feeling? One answer is that the Torah doesn't command the feeling. It commands the table, and the feeling tends to come and sit down. Second, the guest list. The same verse keeps going: thy son, and thy daughter, the servants, the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow. The festival joy is meant to reach people who have no table of their own. Maimonides, the medieval teacher, pressed the point hard. Someone who eats and drinks with family and locks the door against the poor and the bitter-hearted, he wrote, isn't rejoicing in a commandment. That's the joy of the stomach. Third, worship. A psalm sung in the morning prayers says: "Serve the LORD with gladness." The word for gladness is simcha. Fourth, the calendar. At the end of the fall festivals comes Simchat Torah, the joy of the Torah, when the reading ends and begins again, and the scrolls are carried around the synagogue with dancing. Joy, in this root, is something you do, and something you do with people.

segments.voice: Let one good thing from the last few days come back, a message that made you laugh, good news, a meal better than it needed to be, and feel it again. Then picture one person who'd be glad to hear it, maybe someone a bit on their own lately, and hold their face in mind. If you pray, you can give thanks for the good thing.

segments.voice: S-M-Ch. Sin, mem, chet: the root of simcha, joy, sameach, glad, and Simchat Torah. Today's word.
Your line: joy. In this root, a simcha is rarely something anyone has alone. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews call a family celebration a simcha; on the festivals the joy is traditionally widened to include guests, the poor and the lonely, and on Simchat Torah the scrolls are carried around the synagogue with singing and dancing.

chat.says: Why do Jewish celebrations always seem to involve inviting so many people?
options: Festival joy in the Torah comes with a guest list: the stranger, orphan and widow too.
Because in the Torah, joy only counts if a whole synagogue is there.
Mostly custom: big parties came later, and the Torah says little about joy.
